title: India-UK Free Trade Deal Takes Effect, First Zero-Duty Goods Land in London
excerpt: The landmark CETA agreement covering 99% of tariff lines went live on July 15, with the first duty-free jewellery and coffee shipments arriving within 24 hours.
body:
• India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) took effect July 15, 2026, covering 99% of tariff lines and 137 services sub-sectors.
  • First zero-duty shipments — jewellery from Nysa Creations London and Odisha-sourced Kruti Coffee — arrived in the UK on July 16.
  • A Double Contribution Convention exempts over 75,000 Indian workers from dual social security payments, saving an estimated $600 million annually.
  • Both governments target doubling bilateral trade from $65 billion to $100 billion by 2030.

The first consignments of Indian goods to enter Britain at zero duty landed in London on July 16, a day after the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement officially took effect — marking the fastest tangible payoff of a deal three years in the making.

Nysa Creations London shipped the inaugural duty-free jewellery consignment, while Kruti Coffee, a specialty roaster sourcing beans from Odisha, cleared customs without tariffs ahead of its first UK café opening on August 1. The shipments were small but symbolically potent: proof that the agreement's 30 chapters of negotiated text translate into real commercial advantage.

Scale of the Agreement

CETA is India's sixth free trade agreement under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the first with a developed economy. It covers 99 percent of tariff lines and opens 137 services sub-sectors to cross-border competition. The deal spans digital trade, government procurement, and mutual recognition of professional qualifications — areas previous Indian FTAs largely avoided.

"We are targeting to double bilateral trade from $65 billion to $100 billion by 2030. This agreement gives us the architecture to get there."

— P. Kumaran, Indian High Commissioner to the UK

Headline tariff cuts are sharp. Scotch whisky duties fall from 150 percent to 40 percent, a concession that dominated British tabloid coverage of the negotiations. Indian automobile tariffs drop from 100 percent to 10 percent. For India's gem and jewellery sector, the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC) estimates exports to the UK could triple from $754 million to $2.5 billion as duties are phased out.

Economic Impact

Independent projections put the GDP uplift at £4.8 billion for the UK and £5.1 billion for India over the medium term. But the numbers that may matter most to the Indian diaspora in Britain are buried in the agreement's social security provisions.

A Double Contribution Convention, negotiated as part of the deal, exempts more than 75,000 Indian workers in the UK from paying into both countries' social security systems simultaneously. The provision is estimated to save Indian nationals $600 million a year — money that was previously locked into a system most temporary workers never recouped.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the 1.9 million-strong Indian-origin community in Britain, the agreement opens doors on both sides. The 137 services sub-sectors include IT, financial services, and healthcare — industries where Indian professionals are heavily represented. Mutual recognition clauses could eventually ease the credential verification process that has long frustrated Indian-trained doctors, engineers, and accountants seeking to practise in the UK.

"The elimination of duties on gem and jewellery exports could triple our shipments to the UK. This is transformational for small and mid-sized manufacturers in Surat and Mumbai."

— GJEPC spokesperson

The café economy stands to benefit too. Kruti Coffee's August 1 opening in London will test whether Indian specialty coffee can compete on British high streets without the price disadvantage that tariffs previously imposed. Odisha, not traditionally associated with coffee exports, could gain a foothold in a market that imports over £1 billion worth of coffee annually.

What Comes Next

Implementation will be the harder part. Tariff reductions on sensitive items are phased over five to ten years, and both sides retain safeguard mechanisms that can temporarily reimpose duties if imports surge. India's dairy and agricultural sectors remain largely protected, a red line New Delhi maintained throughout negotiations.

Trade officials on both sides say the first 90 days will be critical for ironing out customs procedures and rules-of-origin documentation. For now, the symbolism of zero-duty jewellery and Odisha coffee clearing British customs carries its own momentum — tangible evidence that the deal is more than paper.
